title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Emily Zhao
content:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's engineering standards for service architecture, API design, code hygiene, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance SLOs, and the ADR (architecture decision record) process. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers designing or changing platform services and model-serving components.

Scope

- Applies to all services owned by Engineering (runtime, control plane, telemetry, onboarding pipelines) and to Private/Dedicated deployment packaging.
- Intended readers: service owners, tech leads, SREs, platform engineers, and engineering reviewers.

1) Principles (summary)

- Backwards-compatibility is a first-class concern for public APIs and long-lived internal contracts.
- Design for observability: every service must emit structured traces, metrics, and request-level logs.
- Fail open vs fail closed: user-facing inference requests should degrade gracefully (fallback model variants, reduced max_tokens) rather than return 5xx where possible.
- Automatable and measurable: standards should be machine-testable (linting, CI gates, benchmark harnesses).

2) API Standards (REST/HTTP + grpc guidelines)

Overview:
- Primary public API is JSON-over-HTTP with OpenAPI 3.1 specs. Internal high-throughput RPC between runtime components may use gRPC.

Key rules:
- Use nouns for resources, verbs only for actions that don’t map to resources. Example: POST /v1/requests to create a generation request; POST /v1/requests/{id}:cancel for cancel action.
- Versioning: include API major version in path (e.g., /v1/). Backward-compatible changes go in minor/patch releases.
- Idempotency: long-running operations must accept an Idempotency-Key header.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination (cursor, limit).
- Error model: consistent error object {"code": "string", "message": "string", "details": []}. Use HTTP status codes semantically (400 for client errors, 429 for rate limit, 500 for server errors).
- Rate limiting headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset. Token-level throttles must be surfaced via headers and returned error bodies.
- Authentication: bearer tokens (short-lived) and mTLS for internal control plane traffic.

OpenAPI and SDKs:
- All public endpoints must have an OpenAPI definition checked into the api/ directory of the owning repo. CI must generate SDKs and run integration tests before merging.

3) Coding Standards

Languages in use: Go (services), Python (inference pipelines, evals), TypeScript (console/frontend), Rust/C++ for hot kernels.

Common rules:
- Follow language-specific style guides (gofmt/go vet, black/flake8, prettier/eslint, rustfmt/clippy).
- Mandatory static analysis: lint and type checks in CI. PRs must pass linters and unit tests.
- Module boundaries: keep public API surfaces explicit; prefer small packages and avoid deep import graphs.
- Error handling: prefer explicit error wrapping with context (e.g., fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err) in Go).
- Security coding: validate inputs, avoid unsafe deserialization, and assert authorization at the service boundary.
- Tests: unit tests for logic, integration tests for API contracts, and a lightweight e2e test per service in CI.

4) Infrastructure Standards

Cluster & Networking:
- All services run in Kubernetes (EKS/GKE) for hosted platform; Dedicated/Private packaging uses the same deployment manifests adapted for customer infra.
- Network policies must be defined per namespace; control-plane services are isolated into a dedicated namespace with separate RBAC.

CI/CD:
- GitOps model for infra manifests. Terraform for cloud resources with state locked in S3+Dynamo (or company equivalent).
- Deployments require: automated canary, automated rollback on SLO breach or CI failure, and a manual approval gate for major migrations.

Secrets & Keys:
- KMS-backed secrets in all environments. No secrets in repo. Secrets rotation every 90 days or on compromise.

Capacity & Cost Controls:
- Autoscaling rules must define min/max CPU/GPU nodes and a predictable burst policy for Dedicated customers.

5) Model-serving Standards

Model packaging and versioning:
- Models are stored as versioned artifacts in the model registry (artifact:// model:// style). Each model entry includes metadata: architecture, tokenizer, quantization profile, expected memory, peak VRAM at seq_len 2048, and compatible runtime kernels.
- Model artifacts must ship with a small manifest.json containing: model_id, version, input_schema, output_schema, and quality_checks (list).

Runtime requirements:
- Runtimes must support: streaming token outputs, kv-cache reuse, prefix-caching, and per-request max_tokens enforcement.
- Quantization profiles: defined per model; runtime should expose a quantization_hint header when falling back to a quantized runtime.

Canary & Rollout for model updates:
1. Deploy model variant to 1% traffic for 24-48 hours.
2. Monitor quality metrics (per-prompt evals), latency, and error rates.
3. If metrics within thresholds, progress to 10% -> 50% -> 100%, pausing at each step for at least one evaluation window.
4. Automated rollback trigger: +10% relative regression in quality or >3x increase in tail latency or error rate crossing SLO.

6) Observability Standards

Tracing, metrics, logs:
- Traces: OpenTelemetry instrumentation required for all services. Spans must include service, operation, model_id, request_id, and customer_id (where applicable) as attributes.
- Metrics: Prometheus exposition. Required metrics per service: request_rate, request_latency_ms_p50/p90/p99, request_errors_total (labels: code), model_inference_tokens_generated, gpu_utilization_percent.
- Logs: structured JSON logs at INFO/ERROR. Include request_id and span_id. Logs must avoid PII and must be scrubbed by logging utilities.

Dashboards & Alerts:
- Every service must ship a default dashboard showing throughput, latency p50/p90/p99, error rate, and CPU/GPU utilization.
- Alert thresholds (default):
  - Error budget burn: page when 1-hour error budget burn rate > 50%.
  - Latency: page when p99 latency exceeds SLO by > 25% for 10 minutes.
  - GPU OOM: page on OOM errors.

7) Performance Standards and SLOs

Platform SLOs (hosted):
- Availability: 99.95% for API control plane and management APIs.
- Inference request success rate: 99.9% (excludes client-caused malformed requests).
- Tail latency SLOs (per model-class):
  - Small models (<= 7B): p99 < 300ms for <=256 tokens.
  - Medium models (7B-30B): p99 < 800ms for <=512 tokens.
  - Large models (>30B): p99 < 1500ms for <=1024 tokens.

Benchmarking process:
- Use the benchmarking-and-perf-suite to run representative mixes (50% short, 30% medium, 20% long sequences) and report cost-per-token and tail latency. Every PR that changes runtime kernels must run the benchmark baseline and publish the results.

Optimization levers:
- Batching: configure dynamic batching windows with max latency budget per model class. Default batch windows: small=10ms, medium=15ms, large=25ms.
- KV cache TTL and prefix caching: recommend TTL=24h for repeated prompts within interactive sessions.
- Quantization: recommend quantized variants for cost-sensitive Dedicated tiers; evaluate quality regressions on standard prompt sets.

8) ADR Process (Decision Records)

Purpose:
- Maintain an auditable history of major architecture decisions, alternatives considered, owners, and consequences.

Template (one ADR per decision):
- ADR ID: YYYY-NNN
- Title
- Date
- Status: proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated
- Context: why decision is needed
- Decision: what we decided
- Consequences: operational and technical implications
- Alternatives considered
- Owner(s)

Process:
1. Author drafts ADR in markdown and places in the repo: /docs/adrs/ with filename YYYY-NNN-title.md.
2. Ping reviewers (owners and SRE) and create a PR.
3. Review period: minimum 3 business days.
4. Merge requires at least one engineering lead approval and SRE sign-off for infra-impacting decisions.
5. When accepted, add a reference link from the corresponding Confluence page and update related architecture docs.

Appendix A: Example model manifest (manifest.json)

{
  "model_id": "redwood/rlhf-7b",
  "version": "2026-01-15",
  "architecture": "transformer-decoder",
  "tokenizer": "byte-level-bpe",
  "quantization_profiles": ["int8-q4_0", "fp16"],
  "memory_estimate_bytes_at_seq2048": "28GB",
  "expected_peak_vram": "30GB",
  "runtime_kernels": ["cuda-fused-attn-v2", "kvcache-optimized"],
  "quality_checks": ["perplexity<20", "pass-safety-filters"]
}

Appendix B: Rollout checklist (for infra or model changes)

1. Create change ticket and link ADR (if new decision).
2. Run CI + perf harness and attach results.
3. Deploy to staging; run smoke tests and synthetic traffic for 1 hour.
4. Canary to 1% and monitor metrics for 24h.
5. Gradually increase traffic with step checks.
6. Post-deploy: run regressions on a curated prompt set and notify interested parties via #eng-release-notes.

Governance & Ownership

- Standards owner: Architecture and Standards guild (rotating chair). Guild maintains this page and the ADR index.
- Service owners: each service must register an on-call rotation and an owner in the service README.
- Audit cadence: quarterly review of SLOs, alert thresholds, and ADRs for deprecation.
